Although this is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design with PM2.5 as part of the exposure (AQHI includes PM2.5) and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals, the outcome is urticaria (a skin condition), not respiratory hospitalization or ED visits. This fails to meet the outcome inclusion criterion.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5 from wildfire smoke, (3) outcome includes emergency department visits for asthma (a respiratory condition), (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals. While the study also examines office visits and medication fills, it specifically reports ED visits for asthma which qualifies as respiratory ED visits.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using electronic medical records, (2) exposure includes PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations and emergency visits for asthma exacerbations, (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals for PM2.5 effects, and (6) published in English. The outcome encompasses office, urgent, emergency, and hospitalization visits for asthma, which includes the respiratory hospitalization/ED visits of interest.

This is a time series study examining PM2.5 exposure and pneumonia hospitalizations (a respiratory outcome). While a prevalence ratio of 2.4 is mentioned, it appears to relate to seasonal differences rather than PM2.5 exposure specifically. The PM2.5 association is described only as a correlation coefficient (0.11) and descriptive statistics of PM2.5 levels on admission vs non-admission days. Without access to the full text to confirm whether proper effect estimates with CIs for PM2.5 are reported, the decision remains uncertain.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure, reports respiratory hospital admissions as the outcome, provides relative risk estimates with 95% confidence intervals, and appears to be published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 and pneumonia hospitalizations, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization (pneumonia is a respiratory condition), (4) uses case-crossover design, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates (4.9% and 10.7% risk reductions), and (6) published in English. While the focus is on comparing exposure-response functions and estimating costs, it is still an original epidemiological analysis with appropriate design and effect measures.

This is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design examining PM2.5 exposure and hospitalization outcomes including respiratory disease hospitalizations. While the study also examines all-cause and cardiovascular hospitalizations, it explicitly includes respiratory disease hospitalizations as an outcome. The study reports rate ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Although specific effect estimates for respiratory hospitalizations alone are not provided in the abstract, the methods clearly state this outcome was measured, making it likely reported in the full text.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original time-series epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is AECOPD hospitalizations which is a respiratory hospitalization, (4) uses time-series design with generalized linear model, (5) reports quantitative effect estimate with 95% CI (1.05% increase per 10 μg/m3, 95% CI: 0.14%, 1.96%), and (6) published in English. AECOPD hospitalizations are a specific type of respiratory hospitalization that fits the review's outcome criteria.

Although this is an original case-crossover study examining PM2.5 exposure with quantitative effect estimates, the outcome is myocardial infarction (cardiovascular hospitalization), not respiratory hospitalization or ED visit. This does not meet the inclusion criteria for a systematic review on respiratory hospitalizations.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory hospitalizations (asthma) in children. It reports quantitative effect estimates (percent increases with 95% CI implied) for PM2.5 exposure. Asthma hospitalizations are a respiratory outcome that meets inclusion criteria. The study uses appropriate epidemiological methods (generalized additive model) and appears to be published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using time-series design, examines PM2.5 exposure, reports respiratory hospitalizations as an outcome (along with cardiovascular), and provides quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals (1.05% increase per 10-μg/m³ PM2.5 with 95% posterior interval: 0.29, 1.82 for respiratory hospitalizations).

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) exposure includes PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalizations, (4) uses time-series design with Poisson regression, (5) reports relative risk with 95% confidence intervals (31.8% increase in hospitalization risk per 3.5 µg/m3 increase in PM2.5), and (6) published in English. Although PM2.5 concentrations were estimated by mathematical modeling rather than direct measurement, this does not violate inclusion criteria.

The study examines PM10 (particulate matter ≤10 µm), not PM2.5 (particulate matter ≤2.5 µm). PM10 and PM2.5 are distinct exposure categories with different particle size cutoffs.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure, reports respiratory hospitalizations (COPD admissions) as the outcome, and provides quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (12% increase with 95% CI = 8-16% for warm days and 3% increase with 95% CI = 0-7% for cool days).

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using retrospective analysis; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) the outcome is respiratory disease hospitalization (inpatient data); (4) the study design is time-series analysis using generalized Poisson regression; (5) it reports relative risk (RR) values with specific estimates (RR=1.058 for PM2.5 at lag07d); (6) the article appears to be published in English. While the study examines multiple pollutants, PM2.5 is specifically analyzed and reported.

This is an original epidemiological study using a time-series design with Poisson generalized linear models to examine the association between multiple air pollutants including PM2.5 and respiratory ED visits. The study examines respiratory disease outcomes including asthma ED visits, uses a time-series framework, includes PM2.5 as one of multiple exposures analyzed, and reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., 5.9% of RD ED visits prevented with 95% interval estimate: -0.4% to 12.3%). While the study focuses on regulatory impacts and examines multiple pollutants jointly, it meets the core inclusion criteria as it provides effect estimates for PM2.5 exposure on respiratory ED visits using an appropriate study design.

Although this is an original case-crossover study that includes PM2.5 as an exposure and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals, the outcome is cardiovascular hospitalization (atrial fibrillation) rather than respiratory hospitalization or ED visits. This does not meet the inclusion criteria for a systematic review on PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Original epidemiological study using generalized additive model for time-series analysis; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of multiple exposures; (3) Outcome is COPD hospital admissions, which is a respiratory hospitalization; (4) Time-series design analyzing daily admissions; (5) Reports percentage changes with 95% CIs for PM2.5 (0.82%, 95% CI: 0.38%-1.26%); (6) Published in English. COPD admissions are a specific type of respiratory hospitalization relevant to the review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly studied as one of the exposures, (3) the outcome is respiratory hospitalizations, (4) the study design is case-crossover, (5) effect estimates with confidence intervals are reported (hazard ratios with 95% CIs are mentioned for ozone, and PM2.5 associations are also reported), and (6) the article is in English. While the abstract focuses more on ozone results, it clearly states that PM2.5 was also associated with admissions and that comparisons were made for both pollutants.

This is an original epidemiological study using time-series design that includes PM2.5 as one of multiple exposures. The outcomes include respiratory ED visits (asthma and URI) which meet inclusion criteria. The study reports quantitative effect estimates (2-5% increases) with statistical significance noted. While it is a multipollutant study rather than PM2.5-specific, PM2.5 is explicitly included in the exposure assessment and the inclusion criteria allow for PM2.5 as one of multiple exposures analyzed.

This is a methods/program development paper describing the creation of tools and approaches for future analyses, not an original epidemiological study reporting quantitative effect estimates. The abstract describes 'developing' methods and 'pilot projects' to demonstrate feasibility, and states the program 'will explore ways' to combine results. No actual effect estimates (RR, OR, or CI) are reported for the association between PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations.

This study meets several inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological time-series study with quantitative effect estimates (IRRs with 95% CIs). PM2.5 is mentioned as one of the exposures collected. The abstract does not clearly report PM2.5-specific results for respiratory outcomes. Without access to the full text to confirm whether PM2.5 results for respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits are reported, the decision is uncertain.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory hospitalizations in children. The study reports relative risk estimates and uses DLNM methodology. This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory hospital admissions in children. The study reports quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals (RR with 95% CI mentioned for PM10, and associations described for PM2.5). The outcome is respiratory hospitalization (asthma and wheezing-associated lower respiratory infections), which meets inclusion criteria. Although the abstract primarily highlights NO2 and PM10 results, PM2.5 is explicitly mentioned as one of the exposures analyzed with non-linear associations detected.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is AECOPD hospitalizations which are respiratory hospitalizations, (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports risk estimates for different pollutant concentrations and mentions 'stratified related risks', and (6) published in English. The study examines multiple air pollutants including PM2.5, which is acceptable per inclusion criteria.

The primary exposure is ozone (O3), not PM2.5. While multiple pollutants are analyzed, PM2.5 is specifically included, which satisfies the exposure criterion.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-stratified case-crossover design; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly measured as one of the exposures; (3) the outcome is pneumonia hospital admission, which is a respiratory hospitalization; (4) the study design is case-crossover; (5) odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals are reported (e.g., OR=1.043, 95% CI: 1.004-1.083 for PM2.5); and (6) the article appears to be published in English. While the study focuses on a specific subpopulation (COPD patients), this does not disqualify it from inclusion as it still examines respiratory hospitalizations.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly listed among the air pollutants analyzed, (3) outcome is asthma hospitalization in children (respiratory hospitalization), (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) mentions associations and risk estimates were identified using conditional logistic regression, implying effect estimates with confidence intervals were reported, and (6) published in English. Although multiple pollutants were examined, PM2.5 is specifically included as one of the exposures.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series analysis, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of the exposures, (3) outcome is hospital visits for respiratory infections which qualifies as respiratory hospitalization, (4) time-series design is clearly stated, (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs are reported (PM2.5 ER = 3.46, 95% CI 2.18, 4.76), and (6) published in English. Although multiple pollutants are analyzed, PM2.5 is specifically included and reported.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-stratified case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) the outcome is respiratory hospital admissions, (4) the study design is case-crossover, (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals are reported (0.26% increase per 10 μg/m3 PM2.5 with 95%CI: 0.17%, 0.35%), and (6) the article appears to be published in English. Although the study examines multiple pollutants and effect modification by GDP and greenness, it directly addresses the association between PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations with appropriate quantitative estimates.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using time-series analysis; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) the outcome is respiratory hospitalizations (pneumonia and bronchitis); (4) the study design is time-series with generalized additive models; (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals are reported (e.g., 0.79% increase per 10 μg/m3 PM2.5); (6) the article appears to be published in English based on the abstract provided.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series regression, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory emergency room visits, (4) time-series study design, (5) reports rate ratios with confidence intervals for respiratory ER visits, and (6) published in English. While the study also examines mortality outcomes, it explicitly reports results for respiratory ER visits which meets the outcome criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of multiple exposures, (3) outcome is hospital visits for pneumonia which is a respiratory hospitalization, (4) case-crossover design is clearly stated, (5) odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals are reported (e.g., 6.4% increase, 95%CI 2.3-10.7% for PM2.5), and (6) published in English. Pneumonia is a respiratory condition requiring hospitalization, making this appropriate for the review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5 from wildfire smoke, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations (all respiratory, asthma, COPD), (4) uses case-crossover design (time-stratified), (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) published in English. While the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it clearly reports on respiratory hospitalizations which is the outcome of interest.

The study does not report effect estimates (RR, OR, or equivalent) for the association between PM2.5 concentrations and respiratory hospitalizations, which is the focus of the systematic review. This is an intervention evaluation study rather than an epidemiological study of PM2.5-health associations.

The study examines PM10 (particulate matter ≤10 µm) exposure, not PM2.5 (≤2.5 µm). The study examines ultrafine particles (UFPs; diameter <0.1 μm) as the exposure, not PM2.5 (≤2.5 μm). While this study meets most inclusion criteria (original epidemiological study, PM2.5 exposure, time-series design, quantitative effect estimates with CIs), the outcome is hospital outpatient visits rather than hospitalizations or emergency department visits. This is an original epidemiological study that includes time series analysis examining the association between fine PM (<2.5 μm, which is PM2.5) and pediatric asthma ED visits. The outcome (asthma ED visits) is a respiratory emergency department visit, meeting inclusion criteria.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure and hospitalizations with quantitative effect estimates, the outcome is COVID-19 hospitalization, not respiratory hospitalization in general. The exposure is secondhand smoke (measured by serum cotinine), not PM2.5 or fine particulate matter. While secondhand smoke contains PM2.5, this study specifically examines secondhand smoke exposure as the primary exposure variable, not ambient PM2.5. Additionally, the study design appears to be cross-sectional using NHANES survey data, not time-series or case-crossover as required by inclusion criteria.

While this is an original time-series study examining respiratory hospitalizations (COPD) with effect estimates, the primary exposure is carbon monoxide, not PM2.5. Although PM2.5 is mentioned as a co-pollutant used for adjustment in the analysis, it is not the main exposure of interest. The study focuses on the association between carbon monoxide and COPD hospitalizations.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure and includes hospitalized asthma patients with quantitative effect estimates, the outcome is length of hospital stay (LOS) rather than hospitalization or ED visit incidence. The study design appears to be a cohort or cross-sectional analysis of already hospitalized patients, not a time-series or case-crossover design examining the association between PM2.5 and the occurrence of respiratory hospitalizations.

While this is an original time-series study examining respiratory ED visits with quantitative effect estimates, the exposure is smoke from agricultural burning measured by a potential smoke impact factor (PSIF), not specifically PM2.5 or fine particulate matter. The study does not mention PM2.5 measurement or analysis, which is a required inclusion criterion.

Although the abstract emphasizes CO findings, it explicitly states that PM2.5 was analyzed as one of multiple exposures and was correlated with asthma hospitalizations. Asthma hospitalizations are a respiratory outcome meeting inclusion criteria. The study meets all key inclusion criteria.

While this study meets several inclusion criteria (original epidemiological study, case-crossover design, respiratory hospitalization outcome, reports OR with effect estimate), the exposure is Asian dust (AD) defined by visibility loss, not PM2.5 or fine particulate matter. The abstract does not mention PM2.5 measurement or analysis. Asian dust is a different exposure metric that does not meet the PM2.5 exposure requirement.

While this study meets several inclusion criteria (original epidemiological study, PM2.5 exposure, case-crossover design, reports RR with CI), the outcome is pulmonary embolism hospitalization, which is a cardiovascular/thromboembolic condition, not a respiratory hospitalization. The systematic review specifically targets respiratory hospitalizations, and pulmonary embolism does not fall under this category despite affecting the pulmonary vasculature.

The study examines hospitalization for AECOPD (acute exacerbation of COPD), which is a respiratory outcome, and uses a generalized additive model suggesting a time-series design.
